back: A disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, carried between people by female Anopheles mosquitoes that bite mainly between dusk and dawn.
Parasite development needs temperatures above about 18 °C; mosquitoes breed in standing water; transmission peaks 1–2 months after rain; altitude limits malaria.
Roughly 250 million cases and about 600 000 deaths a year in recent years (WHO, rounded); about 95% in Africa, with young children most at risk.
Seasonal (about November to May); highest in low-lying areas in the north (Zambezi valley), east and south-east lowveld; low on the high plateau.
Insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, rapid diagnostic tests with artemisinin-based treatment, environmental management, education and vaccines for children.
Insecticide and drug resistance, falling funding, nets not used or replaced, conflict and migration, climate change, and remote areas without health services.
The WHO recommended RTS,S (2021) and R21 (2023) for children in areas of moderate to high transmission; roll-out began in several African countries in 2024.
Stable: regular transmission and partial adult immunity, so mainly children are ill. Unstable: irregular transmission and little immunity, so epidemics affect all ages.
